entries.title: Gulf oysters
entries.summary: The eastern oyster of Louisiana's brackish bays: milder and plumper where river water freshens the bay, brinier where the sea pushes in. Eaten raw, chargrilled, fried, baked and in gumbo, and on four Brennan's dishes.
entries.guest: Our Grand Isle Jewels are Louisiana oysters, served raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette: briny, bright and clean.

paras: Gulf oysters are the eastern oyster, Crassostrea virginica, the species of the Atlantic coast and the Gulf. In Louisiana it grows in brackish water, where the Mississippi and the bayous meet the sea, on natural reefs and on leases: patches of state water bottom that a family rents and tends like a field. Most now come from those private leases, a few from the public reefs and a growing number from cages. From 2003 to 2022 Louisiana accounted for about a third of the country's oyster landings.

Salinity, the saltiness of the water, decides the taste. An oyster takes on the water it filters, so a bed freshened by river water and rain gives a milder, plumper oyster, and a bed near the open Gulf gives a brinier, firmer one. The same bed changes with the weather: milder after a wet spring, saltier after a dry autumn. Warm Gulf water grows oysters fast, and the river keeps many beds fresh, so Gulf oysters are known as large and mild.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seabed. Kept off the mud and moved by the tide, they grow cleaner, more even shells, and the farmer can choose saltier water for a brinier oyster. The Grand Isle Jewels grow this way, in floating cages off Grand Isle, a barrier island at the southern edge of Jefferson Parish, where ocean and estuary water mix. Live oysters arrive tightly closed, heavy and smelling of clean sea; a gaping shell that will not close when tapped is dead.

Raw on the half shell, the oyster is shucked to order and sits loose in its liquor, the salty juice in the shell, on crushed ice; the liquor is never poured away. To shuck one, guard the holding hand, pop the hinge with the knife tip, wipe the blade, cut the top muscle, then free the oyster with the cup held level. Cooked, an oyster wants only moments: it is done when its edges, the frilly mantle, begin to curl, and a moment longer shrinks it to a tough button.

Chargrilled oysters go on the half shell over a fierce grill with garlic butter and grated cheese for 3 to 5 minutes, until the butter bubbles and the edges curl. For frying, dredge drained oysters in seasoned cornmeal and fry at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) for 1 to 2 minutes, until golden. Baked, they go back into the shell under a topping: Rockefeller's green herb sauce, or Bienville's shrimp, mushroom and creamy white wine sauce. In gumbo they go in at the very end with their liquor; in oyster dressing, the holiday bread stuffing, they are chopped and baked with onion, celery and green pepper.

The old rule says eat oysters only in months with an R in their name, September to April. It began as common sense before refrigeration: oysters spoiled fast in summer heat, and summer is when they spawn, turning soft, watery and milky. Louisiana's public reefs traditionally opened in September; today the state sets each season's dates and areas.

Today the rule has a modern meaning: warm water lets Vibrio, bacteria that live naturally in Gulf water, multiply, and most illness from raw oysters comes in the warm months. Who is most at risk is taught in the raw and cooked oysters entry; every raw oyster question goes to the manager or the kitchen.

Brennan's serves oysters four ways. The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting, come raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley, briny and bright. The Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch are cooked in New Orleans barbecue sauce, buttery and peppery rather than smoky. Oysters go into the Seafood Gumbo, and smoked oysters into the Creole Caesar's dressing, taking the savoury role anchovy plays. The count per order is a lineup question.

A guest from the East Coast may ask why New Orleans cooks its oysters: Gulf oysters are large and mild, so they take to butter, fire and frying. Steer a guest who wants a briny raw oyster to the Jewels. Tell a guest choosing the Creole Caesar that its dressing is made with smoked oysters; the guide treats it as a shellfish dish, so flag it on the ticket and send shellfish questions to the kitchen. Raw oysters carry the consumer advisory: read the service note and send raw seafood questions to the manager or kitchen.

faults.cause: Cooked past the moment the edges curl, or left simmering in a gumbo.
faults.fix: Cook only until the mantle curls; add them to a soup at the very end, off the boil.

faults.fault: Grit or shell in the mouth
faults.cause: Mud left on the shell, or the knife chipping the hinge as it went in.
faults.fix: Scrub and rinse the shells before shucking, wipe the knife between oysters and check each one by eye.

faults.cause: The liquor spilled in shucking, or the oyster was weak or old.
faults.fix: Keep the cup level as you open it; an oyster that smells off is thrown away, never served.

faults.cause: A summer oyster in spawning condition.
faults.fix: Expect it in the warm months; ask the supplier about the harvest and favour such oysters for cooking.

faults.cause: Oil below 175°C (347°F), or the basket crowded so the oil cooled.
faults.fix: Fry in small batches at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) and drain on a rack.

brennans.how: Off-bottom oysters from Grand Isle's floating cages, shucked raw on the half shell over ice with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley: briny and bright, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting.
Big, mild Louisiana oysters cooked in a buttery, peppery New Orleans barbecue sauce, with pickled collard greens and a fried saltine crumble; how many come per order is a lineup question.

Oysters join the shrimp, crab and smoky andouille of the Seafood Gumbo over popcorn rice; the published recipe adds the seafood at the very end, so confirm at lineup that the dining room gumbo follows it.

Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar dressing, taking the savoury role anchovy usually plays; the house guide treats the salad as a shellfish dish, so flag it on the ticket and leave shellfish and anchovy questions to the kitchen.

cards.front: Which oyster species grows in Louisiana's brackish bays?
cards.back: The eastern oyster, Crassostrea virginica, the same species found along the Atlantic coast, here grown where river water meets the Gulf.

cards.front: Where do most Louisiana oysters come from today?
cards.back: Private leases, patches of state water bottom a family rents and tends; the public reefs give a small share and cages a growing one.

cards.front: How does the saltiness of the water change an oyster's taste?
cards.back: Fresher water from river and rain gives a milder, plumper oyster; saltier water near the open Gulf gives a brinier, firmer one.

cards.front: What is off-bottom oyster farming, and what does it give?
cards.back: Oysters raised in floating or hanging cages above the seabed: kept off the mud, they grow cleaner, more even shells.

cards.front: What did the R-month rule guard against before refrigeration?
cards.back: Oysters spoiling in summer heat on the way to market, and the soft, watery oysters of the spawning season, the months without an R.

cards.front: What is the modern meaning of the R-month rule?
cards.back: Summer oysters are softer from spawning, and warm water lets Vibrio bacteria multiply, so raw oysters carry more risk; questions go to the kitchen.

cards.front: How do you know a cooked oyster is done?
cards.back: Its edges, the frilly mantle, begin to curl; a moment longer and it shrinks and toughens.

cards.front: When do oysters go into a gumbo, and why?
cards.back: At the very end, with their liquor, cooked only until the edges curl, so they stay plump instead of shrinking to rubber.

cards.front: What is oyster liquor, and what happens to it at the raw bar?
cards.back: The salty juice in the shell: part of the taste, kept in the cup when shucking and never poured away.

cards.front: How are Brennan's Grand Isle Jewel Oysters served?
cards.back: Raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting.

cards.front: What does barbecue mean on Brennan's Louisiana Oysters?
cards.back: A buttery, peppery New Orleans pan sauce, not smoke and not tomato, with pickled collard greens and a fried saltine crumble.

cards.front: Why must a server mention the oysters on the Creole Caesar?
cards.back: Its dressing is made with smoked oysters, which guests do not expect in a Caesar; the house guide treats it as a shellfish dish: mention it, flag it on the ticket and send questions to the kitchen.

questions.q: Which species are the oysters grown in Louisiana's brackish bays?

questions.q: An oyster bed freshened by river water and rain will usually give what kind of oyster?
questions.why: An oyster tastes of the water it filters: fresher water makes it mild and plump, saltier water near the open Gulf makes it briny.

distractors: The flavour of the wild reef
A shell that opens by itself
questions.why: Raised above the seabed and moved by the tide, caged oysters stay out of the mud and grow cleaner, more even shells.

questions.q: What is the modern meaning of the old R-month rule?

entries.title: Redfish, drum and the Gulf fish
entries.say: As it reads: redfish, drum, Gulf fish.
entries.summary: Redfish, the red drum, is the Gulf's firm, mild, copper-red fish with a black spot by its tail. Learn it, its cousins and the day's catch, how round and flat fish are cut, and why redfish left commercial nets.
entries.guest: Redfish is the red drum, a firm, mild Gulf fish. Our Gulf fish changes with the day's catch: let me tell you exactly which fish the kitchen has tonight and how it is cooked.

paras: Redfish is the cook's name for the red drum, a fish of the Gulf's bays and shallow coastal water. It is copper red to bronze along the back, paler below, with at least one black spot near the tail. The flesh is white, firm and mild, a little sweet, with a large flake that holds together, so it takes a sear, a sauce or the grill.

Black drum is its larger, coarser cousin: grey to black, with whisker-like barbels under the chin. Smaller black drum eat much like redfish; the very large ones are coarse and seldom kept for the table. The fish on the plate changes with the boats.

Speckled trout, the spotted sea trout, is not a true trout but another drum: soft, delicate and sweet. Flounder is a flat fish with a fine, tender flake. Pompano is small, silver and rich, long prized in the Creole kitchen. Sheepshead, named for its sheep-like teeth, eats crabs and barnacles and has firm, sweet white flesh. Red snapper is firm and sweet under pink skin; grouper is firm with large, moist flakes; tripletail is firm, white and mild. Cobia and amberjack are big, rich, meaty fish, cut into steaks or thick fillets for the grill, with the dark bloodline trimmed away.

A round fish, such as redfish, snapper or trout, has an eye on each side and a backbone down the middle; it gives two fillets. A flat fish, such as flounder, swims on its side with both eyes on top; filleted along the centre line, the classic way, it gives four fillets, two from each side, or it is cooked whole. Skin on, a fillet holds together and can be seared crisp, skin side down, for most of its cooking; skin off, it suits poaching, a papillote (a sealed parcel baked so the fish steams in its own juices) or a crust.

Pin bones are the fine bones in a line down the thicker front half of a round fish fillet. Find them with a fingertip and pull each one with fish tweezers towards the head, the way it lies, so the flesh does not tear.

Fresh fish has clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh that springs back and a clean sea smell; keep it on ice, as near 0°C (32°F) as you can, and use it within a day or two. Cook a fillet until it turns from translucent to opaque and just flakes, 63°C (145°F) at the centre, the figure the USDA gives for fish.

Until the 1980s redfish was an ordinary commercial fish in Louisiana. Around 1980 Paul Prudhomme began serving blackened redfish at K-Paul's in New Orleans and made it famous, and kitchens across the country copied it. The Gulf was fished hard, and the stock fell.

From 1987 federal rules barred a directed commercial redfish fishery in the Gulf's federal waters, and in January 1988 Louisiana banned its commercial harvest too. Red drum is now managed in Louisiana for anglers: state law (R.S. 56:325.3) still prohibits its commercial taking, possession or landing. Redfish on a Louisiana menu today is usually farm raised or comes from outside the state's waters.

Redfish has its own dish at Brennan's: on the Redfish Véronique it stands in for the sole of the French classic, firm enough for a beurre blanc and hibiscus-pickled grapes. Never call it wild Louisiana redfish; where ours comes from is a question for the chef.

The Gulf fish of the day is the day's catch, not one species, on three plates: the Pecan Gulf Fish at breakfast and lunch, the Gulf Fish en Papillote at dinner and the children's sautéed Gulf fish with potato and green beans. Never call the Véronique's redfish the Gulf fish of the day: it is its own fish, with its own story.

Every table asks what the fish is tonight, so learn it at lineup, never guess, and give it with its texture: flaky and delicate, or firm and meaty. If the kitchen has not said, offer to ask. A guest who remembers blackened redfish will enjoy the story of why it left the commercial nets. Questions about bones or allergies are answered from the service note and the kitchen, never from memory.

faults.fault: Fillet breaks up in the pan
faults.cause: A delicate fish such as trout or flounder handled like redfish, or turned before it released.
faults.fix: Match the method to the fish, and let the fillet colour and release before turning it once.

faults.cause: Old fish, or fish kept warm or poorly iced.
faults.fix: Buy fish with clear eyes and red gills, keep it on ice and cook it within a day or two.

faults.fault: A pin bone in the mouth
faults.fix: Run a fingertip down the thick front of every round fish fillet and pull each bone towards the head.
Take it off as it just flakes, about 63°C (145°F) at the centre; it carries on cooking as it rests.

faults.cause: A wet skin or a pan not hot enough.
faults.fix: Pat the skin dry, heat the oil until it shimmers and leave the fillet until it lets go.

brennans.how: Firm, mild redfish stands in for the classic sole, with beurre blanc, hibiscus-pickled grapes and braised leeks; never call it wild Louisiana redfish, and ask the chef where ours comes from.
The day's Gulf catch with Louisiana lump crab, a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens; name today's fish first, learned at lineup.

The day's Gulf fish, wrapped in banana leaf and served with Louisiana crab, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds; what goes inside the leaf, and whether it is opened at the table, is confirmed at lineup.
On the children's dinner, the day's Gulf fish is sautéed in a pan and served with potato and green beans; which fish it is changes, and the kitchen says at lineup.

cards.front: How do you recognise a redfish?
cards.back: Copper red to bronze along the back, paler below, with at least one black spot near the tail; firm, mild white flesh.

cards.front: How does black drum differ from redfish?
cards.back: It grows larger and coarser, grey to black with barbels under the chin; smaller black drum eat much like redfish.

cards.front: What is the speckled trout on a New Orleans menu?
cards.back: The spotted sea trout, not a true trout but a drum: soft, delicate and sweet, so it needs a gentle hand in the pan.

cards.front: What are cobia and amberjack like, and how are they cut for the grill?
cards.back: Big, rich, meaty Gulf fish, cut into steaks or thick fillets, with the dark bloodline trimmed away before they cook.

cards.front: Why is there no wild Louisiana redfish on a menu?
cards.back: The blackening craze drove heavy fishing, Louisiana closed its commercial fishery in the late 1980s, and its commercial taking is still prohibited there.

cards.front: Where does redfish on a Louisiana menu come from today?
cards.back: It is usually farm raised or comes from outside the state's waters; ask the chef where ours comes from.

cards.front: What does Gulf fish of the day mean on the menu?
cards.back: The day's catch from the Gulf, not one species; learn tonight's fish and how it is cooked at lineup, and never guess.

cards.front: How many fillets do a round fish and a flat fish give?
cards.back: A round fish gives two, one from each side; a flat fish, with both eyes on top, gives four when filleted the classic way.

cards.front: How do you take out pin bones?
cards.back: Find them with a fingertip along the thick front of the fillet and pull each with tweezers towards the head, the way it lies.

cards.front: How do you know a fish fillet is cooked?
cards.back: The flesh turns from translucent to opaque and just flakes under gentle pressure, about 63°C (145°F) at the centre.

cards.front: Which Brennan's plates carry the Gulf fish of the day?
cards.back: The Pecan Gulf Fish, the Gulf Fish en Papillote and the children's sautéed Gulf fish with potato and green beans.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish uses redfish, and in place of what?
cards.back: The Redfish Véronique, where redfish stands in for the sole of the French classic, with beurre blanc and hibiscus-pickled grapes.

questions.q: Which mark on its body identifies a redfish?
questions.answer: A black spot near the tail
questions.why: The redfish carries at least one black spot by its tail; barbels mark the black drum, and two eyes on one side a flat fish.

questions.q: Which fish is the redfish's larger, coarser cousin?
questions.why: Black drum belongs to the same drum family and grows larger and coarser; pompano, sheepshead and flounder are other fish altogether.

questions.q: What is the speckled trout of a New Orleans menu?
questions.answer: A drum, the spotted sea trout
distractors: A flat fish, a cousin of flounder
questions.why: Speckled trout is the spotted sea trout, a soft, sweet member of the drum family and no relation to freshwater trout.

questions.q: What happened to Louisiana's commercial redfish fishery after the blackening craze?
questions.answer: It was closed in the late 1980s
distractors: It doubled its catch in the 1990s
It moved offshore to deeper water
It was opened to foreign fleets
questions.why: Heavy fishing drove the stock down, Louisiana closed the commercial fishery, and the commercial taking of red drum there is still prohibited.

questions.q: A guest asks what tonight's Gulf fish is and you did not hear it at lineup. What do you do?
questions.why: The Gulf fish changes with the catch, so a server never guesses; the kitchen gives the species and how it is cooked.

questions.q: Filleted along the centre line, the classic way, how many fillets does a flat fish such as flounder give?
questions.why: A flat fish lies on its side with both eyes on top and gives two fillets from each side; a round fish gives two in all.

questions.q: In which direction do you pull a pin bone from a fillet?
questions.answer: Towards the head, the way it lies
distractors: Towards the tail, against the lie
questions.why: Pulled the way it lies, the bone slides out cleanly; pulled against it, the bone tears the flesh.

questions.q: What centre temperature does the USDA give for cooked fish?
questions.why: At 63°C (145°F) the flesh has turned opaque and just flakes; far beyond it the fillet dries and turns chalky.

questions.q: On the Redfish Véronique, what does the redfish stand in for?
questions.answer: The sole of the French classic
distractors: The shrimp of a Creole sauce
questions.why: Véronique is the French classic of sole with grapes; firm, mild redfish takes the sole's place under the beurre blanc.

questions.q: A guest asks whether our redfish is wild Louisiana redfish. What do you say?
questions.answer: I will ask the chef where ours comes from
distractors: Yes, it was caught off Grand Isle this morning
Yes, all redfish from the Gulf is wild
No, ours is always farmed in Texas
questions.why: Louisiana still prohibits the commercial taking of red drum, so restaurant redfish is farmed or caught elsewhere; where ours comes from is a question for the chef.

entries.title: Andouille
entries.summary: Cajun andouille is a coarse pork sausage, heavy with garlic and pepper and smoked for hours until dark and firm. It is made to season a pot, browned first so its fat and smoke flavour gumbo, jambalaya and red beans.
entries.guest: Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, is Louisiana's coarse, smoked pork sausage, firm and smoky rather than juicy. In our Seafood Gumbo it gives a smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters.

paras: Andouille is south Louisiana's smoked seasoning sausage: pork shoulder and its fat, cut coarse, seasoned hard with garlic, black pepper and cayenne, stuffed into a wide casing and smoked low for hours until it is dark brown and firm. Cut one open and you see big, distinct pieces of meat rather than a fine paste.

It is not a sausage for the grill plate. Firm and smoky rather than juicy, it is made to season a pot, and a little of it carries smoke, salt, fat and heat through a whole gumbo. In Creole and Cajun cooking it works as much as a seasoning as the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper.

Pork shoulder, which runs roughly three parts lean to one of fat, is cut into large dice or ground through a coarse plate, about 10 mm. Season it with salt at 1.75 to 2 per cent of the meat's weight, plenty of fresh garlic, coarse black pepper and cayenne, often a little thyme, and pink curing salt no. 1 (salt with sodium nitrite) at the dose its maker prints. The cure keeps the meat pink and guards against the bacteria that like the low, slow heat of a smokehouse.

Curing salt is weighed to the gram, never guessed, and kept apart from table salt: making andouille is charcutier's work, the craft of the pork butcher and sausage maker, done under a senior cook, while a Commis masters the browning and the timing in the pot.

Mix the seasoned meat until it turns tacky, stuff it firmly and tie it in links. Let the links dry until the surface is tacky, then smoke them low, starting around 60°C (140°F) to dry them and take the smoke, and raise the heat to 75 to 80°C (167 to 176°F) over several hours, traditionally over pecan wood in LaPlace, until the centre reaches 71°C (160°F), the USDA mark for cooked ground pork.

In the pot, cut andouille into half-moons about 1 cm (about ½ inch) thick and brown them in a heavy pot over medium heat for 5 to 8 minutes, until the edges colour and the fat runs. Lift them out: the smoky fat now flavours the roux or the trinity. In a brown jambalaya the browned bits on the bottom of the pot colour the rice; in red beans the andouille simmers for hours with the beans. Return it to simmer so its smoke spreads through the liquid.

French andouille is a different thing. Andouille de Vire from Normandy and andouille de Guémené from Brittany are made from the pig's chitterlings, its intestines and stomach, smoked and cooked, then sliced cold; the Guémené shows neat rings when cut. Andouillette is the smaller cousin, chitterlings and often tripe, grilled hot and served with mustard, with a strong, farmyard smell. Louisiana kept the name and the smoke and filled the casing with shoulder meat instead, so warn a guest who expects the French one before they order.

Louisiana andouille is a River Parishes sausage. The German farmers of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, brought a strong tradition of sausage making, with French, Acadian and other influences beside it. The town that made it famous is LaPlace, in St. John the Baptist Parish, which calls itself the Andouille Capital of the World: Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the title in the 1970s, and the first Andouille Festival was held there in October 1972; today the parish runs it each October. LaPlace andouille is known for its pecan wood smoke.

Unbrowned andouille dropped into a finished pot stays rubbery and gives little; browned first, it gives its fat and smoke to everything after it. Scorched edges taste bitter, so keep the heat at medium. Andouille brings its own salt and pepper, so a gumbo salted before the sausage has simmered is easily oversalted: season at the end.

At Brennan's andouille is in the Seafood Gumbo, the smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters, served over popcorn rice. The menu names no maker: never say ours is from LaPlace or from a named smokehouse unless the kitchen confirms it.

Say ahn-DOO-ee. Describe it as a coarse, smoked pork sausage, firm and smoky, that seasons the gumbo. Andouille is pork, so tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order. Questions about anything else in the bowl go to the service note and the kitchen.

ratios.value: As its maker prints, commonly 2.5 g per 1 kg (2.2 lb)

faults.cause: Andouille added unbrowned, late in the cooking.
faults.fix: Brown it first until the fat runs, then simmer it in the liquid.

faults.cause: Browned over too high a heat.
faults.fix: Brown over medium heat and stir; lower the heat once the fat runs.

faults.cause: Salted before the andouille had given up its own salt.
faults.fix: Taste and season at the end of the simmer.

faults.cause: Too much rendered fat left in.
faults.fix: Pour off some fat after browning, and skim the surface as it simmers.

cards.front: How is andouille used in Louisiana cooking?
cards.back: As a seasoning: a little, browned first, carries smoke, salt, fat and heat through gumbo, jambalaya and red beans.

cards.front: Which town calls itself the Andouille Capital of the World?
cards.back: LaPlace, in St. John the Baptist Parish; Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the title in the 1970s, and its festival dates from 1972.

cards.front: Which settlers shaped andouille making in the River Parishes?
cards.back: The German farmers of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, with French, Acadian and other influences beside them.

cards.front: How does French andouille differ from Cajun andouille?
cards.back: French andouille and andouillette are chitterling sausages, made from the pig's intestines and stomach; Cajun andouille is smoked shoulder meat.

cards.front: What do you tell a guest who expects French andouillette?
cards.back: That Louisiana andouille is a smoked pork shoulder sausage, not a chitterling sausage, so they know what will arrive before they order.

cards.front: Why is andouille browned before the gumbo is built?
cards.back: Browning renders its fat and smoke into the pot to flavour the roux or the trinity; unbrowned slices stay rubbery and give little.

cards.front: Why is a pot with andouille salted only at the end?
cards.back: Andouille gives its own salt and pepper to the liquid as it simmers, so salting early can leave the pot oversalted.

cards.front: What centre temperature does smoked andouille reach?
cards.back: 71°C (160°F), the USDA mark for cooked ground pork, reached slowly in low smoke over several hours.

cards.front: Where is andouille on the Brennan's menu?
cards.back: In the Seafood Gumbo, its smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters, over popcorn rice; the menu names no maker.

cards.front: What must a guest who avoids pork hear about the Seafood Gumbo?
cards.back: That it carries andouille, a pork sausage, told before they order, with any other question sent to the kitchen.

cards.front: How do you say andouille, and how do you describe it to a guest?
cards.back: ahn-DOO-ee. A coarse, smoked pork sausage, firm and smoky rather than juicy, that seasons the Seafood Gumbo.

questions.q: What is Cajun andouille made from?
questions.why: Cajun andouille is coarse shoulder meat and fat, smoked; chitterlings make the French andouille, and rice with liver makes boudin.

questions.q: Which town calls itself the Andouille Capital of the World?
questions.why: LaPlace, on the river in St. John the Baptist Parish, carries the title a governor proclaimed in the 1970s.

questions.q: Which settlers of the River Parishes brought a strong sausage-making tradition?
questions.answer: German farmers of the German Coast
distractors: Italian grocers of the French Quarter
English traders of the Gulf coast
questions.why: The German Coast upriver from New Orleans was farmed by German settlers, whose sausage making shaped Louisiana andouille.

questions.q: A guest says they love French andouillette. What should you explain before they order?
distractors: Ours is the same French sausage
Ours is made with blood and rice
Ours is a fresh, unsmoked sausage
questions.why: French andouille and andouillette are chitterling sausages; Louisiana kept the name and the smoke and uses shoulder meat.

questions.q: Why is andouille browned at the start of a gumbo?
questions.answer: Its fat and smoke season the pot
questions.why: Browned first, andouille renders smoky fat that flavours the roux or the trinity and everything after it.

questions.q: Why is a pot with andouille seasoned with salt at the end?
questions.answer: The sausage gives up its own salt
questions.why: Andouille releases salt and pepper as it simmers, so the pot is tasted and seasoned only once it has done so.

questions.q: What centre temperature marks cooked ground pork, the target for smoked andouille?
questions.why: The USDA gives 71°C (160°F) for ground pork; 63°C (145°F) is its figure for whole cuts, not sausage.

questions.q: Which dish on the Brennan's menu carries andouille?
questions.why: Andouille is the smoky backbone of the Seafood Gumbo, with shrimp, crab and oysters over popcorn rice.

questions.q: A guest who avoids pork is choosing between the soups. What must they hear about the Seafood Gumbo?
questions.answer: It carries andouille, a pork sausage
distractors: It is made with seafood alone
Its andouille is a chicken sausage
Nothing, unless they ask about spice
questions.why: Andouille is pork and the smoky backbone of the gumbo, so a guest who avoids pork hears it before ordering; any other question goes to the kitchen.

questions.q: A guest points to andouille on the menu and asks how to say it. What do you tell them?
questions.why: Say ahn-DOO-ee, as the house guide writes it, then describe it as a coarse, smoked pork sausage that seasons the gumbo.

entries.title: Tasso
entries.say: TAH-so (TASS-oh is also heard; confirm the house habit)
entries.summary: Tasso is Cajun seasoning meat: strips of pork shoulder briefly cured, coated in cayenne, garlic and spice, and hot-smoked until firm. Diced small, a little seasons a whole pot of beans, gumbo or Creole sauce.
entries.guest: Tasso, TAH-so, is Cajun smoked pork shoulder, spiced with cayenne and garlic. It seasons our Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits, so the sauce is smoky as well as tangy.

paras: Tasso is south Louisiana's seasoning meat. Cooks cut strips of pork shoulder, cure them briefly in salt and sugar, coat them thickly in cayenne, garlic and other spices, and hot-smoke them until firm and cooked through. It is sometimes called Cajun ham, but the name misleads: it comes from the shoulder, not the hind leg, and it is far too spicy and smoky to slice and eat like ham.

A little does a great deal: diced and cooked into a dish, tasso spreads smoke, salt and heat through the whole pot. It is tied by tradition to the boucherie, the communal hog killing of Acadiana, where neighbours shared every part of the pig and lean trimmings became seasoning meat.

Cut pork shoulder (the butt) across the grain into strips about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick, trimming the heaviest fat. Cure them in salt and sugar with pink curing salt no. 1 at the dose its maker prints. The boucherie's cure is brief, three or four hours; many modern makers dry-cure the strips in the fridge for a day or two, measuring salt at 2 to 2.5 per cent of the meat's weight. Rinse, pat dry and coat every side thickly with the rub: cayenne, paprika, black and white pepper and garlic, often with thyme, marjoram or allspice.

Leave the strips uncovered in the fridge until the surface is dry and tacky, a few hours or overnight, so the smoke clings. Hot-smoke them over pecan, hickory or oak at about 95 to 110°C (203 to 230°F) for 2 to 4 hours, until the centre reaches at least 63°C (145°F), the USDA mark for whole cuts of pork; many smokehouses take it to around 68°C (155°F) for a firmer piece. Cool, wrap and keep it chilled; it freezes well in small portions.

Tasso is used by the spoonful, not the slice. Dice it small, about 5 mm (¼ inch), and render it gently, cooking it slowly so its fat melts out, in a little butter or oil over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes before the trinity goes in, so the spices bloom without scorching. As a rough measure, 115 g (4 oz) of diced tasso seasons about 1 litre (about 1 quart) of Creole sauce, beans or gumbo. For a cream sauce for pasta, the cream is reduced over the browned tasso until it coats a spoon. Season every dish only at the end: tasso brings its own salt.

Country ham is a different thing from the same pig: the hind leg, dry-cured in salt for weeks and aged for months, often smoked, and eaten in thin slices or fried; it is salty and deep rather than hot. Tasso is the shoulder, cured for hours or days, hot-smoked until cooked and coated in pepper, a seasoning rather than a slice. Andouille is a sausage, coarse chopped meat and fat in a casing, garlicky where tasso is lean and fiery, though both are browned to season a pot.

Tasso fails in the pan more often than in the smokehouse. Thick pieces give a mouthful of salt and cayenne; the pepper crust scorches at high heat and turns bitter; added cold at the end, it never gives its smoke to the liquid.

At Brennan's tasso seasons the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, a breakfast and lunch entrée: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato sauce built on the holy trinity, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake with fried okra chips. The tasso makes the sauce smoky as well as tangy. The menu names no maker, so ask the kitchen before saying it is smoked in-house or bought from a named smokehouse.

Both TAH-so and TASS-oh are heard in Louisiana; the house guide writes TAH-so, so confirm the house habit and follow it. If a guest calls it Cajun ham, explain that it is shoulder, not leg, a seasoning meat. Tasso is pork, so flag it for a guest who avoids pork before they order the Shrimp & Grits, and tell them the house guide rates the dish mild to moderate in spice.

ratios.label: Salt in a measured dry cure
Pink curing salt no. 1
ratios.value: As its maker prints, commonly 2.5 g per 1 kg (2.2 lb)

ratios.label: Diced tasso to sauce, beans or gumbo
ratios.value: About 115 g (4 oz) to 1 litre (about 1 quart)

temps.label: Centre at least, the USDA mark for whole cuts of pork
Centre for a firmer, drier piece

faults.fault: A mouthful of salt and cayenne
faults.cause: Tasso cut in thick pieces or slices, like ham.
faults.fix: Dice it small, about 5 mm (¼ inch), so it spreads through the dish.

faults.fault: Bitter, burnt edge on the sauce
faults.cause: The spice crust scorched over high heat.
faults.fix: Render it gently over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, then add the trinity to cool the pan.

faults.cause: Tasso stirred in cold at the end.
faults.fix: Render it first and let it simmer in the sauce so its smoke and spice reach the liquid.

faults.cause: Salted before the tasso had given up its own salt.
faults.fix: Taste and season only at the end.

brennans.how: Tasso seasons the Creole sauce over the Louisiana shrimp and fried pimento cheese grit cake, making it smoky as well as tangy; the menu names no maker, so ask the kitchen.

cards.front: What is tasso, in plain words?
cards.back: Strips of pork shoulder briefly cured, coated in cayenne, garlic and spice, and hot-smoked until firm: a seasoning meat, not a ham.

cards.front: Why is Cajun ham a misleading name for tasso?
cards.back: Ham is the hind leg; tasso is cut from the shoulder, and it is too spicy and smoky to slice and eat like ham.

cards.front: Where did tasso come from?
cards.back: The boucherie, the communal hog killing of Acadiana: by tradition, tasso was made there from the last lean pieces, as a seasoning meat.

cards.front: How is tasso smoked, and to what centre temperature?
cards.back: Hot-smoked at about 95 to 110°C (203 to 230°F) until the centre reaches at least 63°C (145°F), the USDA mark for whole cuts of pork.

cards.front: How is tasso prepared for a sauce?
cards.back: Diced small, about 5 mm (¼ inch), and rendered gently in a little fat before the trinity, so its spices bloom without scorching.

cards.front: Roughly how much diced tasso seasons 1 litre (about 1 quart) of sauce or beans?
cards.back: About 115 g (4 oz); it brings salt, smoke and heat, so the dish is seasoned only at the end.

cards.front: How do you say tasso?
cards.back: TAH-so; TASS-oh is also heard in Louisiana, so confirm the house habit and follow it.

cards.front: How does tasso differ from country ham?
cards.back: Country ham is the hind leg, salt-cured for weeks and aged for months, eaten sliced; tasso is shoulder, cured briefly, hot-smoked and used to season.

cards.front: How does tasso differ from andouille?
cards.back: Andouille is a coarse, garlicky sausage in a casing; tasso is whole strips of lean shoulder under a fiery spice crust.

cards.front: Where is tasso on the Brennan's menu?
cards.back: In the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, making the tomato sauce smoky as well as tangy.

cards.front: A guest asks who makes our tasso. What do you say?
cards.back: The menu names no maker, so offer to ask the kitchen rather than claiming it is smoked in-house or bought in.

questions.q: From which cut of the pig is tasso made?
questions.why: Tasso is cut from the shoulder; the hind leg makes ham, which is why Cajun ham is a misleading name.

questions.q: Tasso comes from the boucherie. What was a boucherie?
questions.why: At the boucherie, neighbours in Acadiana butchered a hog together and shared every part; by tradition, tasso was made from the last lean pieces.

questions.q: What is the minimum centre temperature for hot-smoked tasso, a whole cut of pork?
questions.why: The USDA gives 63°C (145°F) for whole cuts of pork; many smokehouses go a little higher for a firmer piece.

questions.q: Why is diced tasso rendered gently before the trinity goes in?
questions.answer: So its spices bloom, not scorch
distractors: So it crisps hard like fried bacon
So most of its salt cooks away
So its fat thickens the sauce
questions.why: Gentle heat draws out the smoke and spice into the fat; high heat burns the cayenne crust and turns it bitter.

questions.q: Roughly how much diced tasso seasons 1 litre (about 1 quart) of Creole sauce or beans?
questions.why: Tasso is a seasoning meat used by the spoonful: about 115 g (4 oz) carries smoke, salt and heat through a litre, and the dish is salted only at the end.

questions.q: How should a server say tasso at Brennan's?
questions.answer: Follow the house habit, usually TAH-so
distractors: tah-SOH, stressed at the end as in French
Avoid the word and call it Cajun ham
questions.why: Both TAH-so and TASS-oh are heard in Louisiana; the house guide writes TAH-so, and the server confirms the house habit.

questions.q: Which of these describes country ham rather than tasso?
questions.answer: A hind leg salt-cured and aged for months
distractors: A shoulder strip hot-smoked in hours
A spiced seasoning meat diced small
A cayenne crust over lean pork
questions.why: Country ham is the hind leg, cured for weeks and aged for months; tasso is quick-cured, hot-smoked shoulder used to season.

questions.q: Which Brennan's sauce does tasso season?
questions.answer: The Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits
distractors: The marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde
The beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique
The pecan bordelaise on the Gulf fish
questions.why: Tasso seasons the Creole sauce over the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, giving the tomato sauce its smoke.
